sections.heading: Owning my sin before your holy law
sections.text: Father, you are holy and your commands are good. I am ashamed of how I have sinned against you—not only in ways other people could see, but in the hidden places of my heart. I have left undone what I should have done. I have gone through worship and prayer and hearing your Word without love, attention, or faith. Even the things I call “spiritual” have been mixed with selfishness, distraction, pride, and coldness. I will not excuse myself before you.
theological_themes: God’s law is good and exposes real guilt.
Sin includes outward acts, hidden faults, neglected obedience, and corrupted worship.
True repentance begins with honest confession rather than self-defense.

scripture_references.connection: David asks God to cleanse him from hidden faults and keep him from deliberate sins, which fits this confession of both visible disobedience and secret corruption.
James teaches that failing to do the good one knows to do is itself sin, grounding the prayer’s confession of neglected duties and missed obedience.

sections.heading: Looking to Christ where my guilt is known
sections.text: My sins are not small, and they are not hidden from heaven. They rise higher than I can manage or explain away. But Jesus is there too. He stands for me before you as my Advocate. His sacrifice is enough for my sins. So even while I confess honestly, I listen for the peace that comes from him, not from my performance.
theological_themes: God fully knows sin; nothing is concealed from him.
Christ intercedes for sinners before the Father.
Forgiveness and peace rest on Christ’s atoning sacrifice, not on personal improvement.

scripture_references.connection: John holds together honest acknowledgement of sin with the comfort that Jesus Christ is the believer’s Advocate and the propitiation for sins.
Hebrews says Christ appears in God’s presence on behalf of his people, supporting the prayer’s confidence that Christ is in heaven representing the sinner.

sections.heading: Admitting how little I have received from you
sections.text: Right now, what is alive in me feels small. I have enough light to see how dark I can be. I have enough tenderness to notice how hard my heart still is. I have enough spiritual hunger to grieve that my mind and desires are so often stuck on earthly things. But I cannot pretend this is all you offered me. You have never been the narrow place. You have held out full mercy, full wisdom, full strength, and full life in Christ. I have lived on crumbs when you invited me to come and receive from your abundance.
theological_themes: Spiritual awareness itself is a mercy, even when it reveals weakness.
Believers may be slow, cold, and underdeveloped in grace.
God’s fullness in Christ is not deficient; the poverty is in our unbelief and neglect.

scripture_references.connection: John speaks of believers receiving grace from Christ’s fullness, which grounds the prayer’s claim that God has not been lacking in what he offers.
Paul calls believers to set their minds on things above, illuminating the prayer’s sorrow over having too little of a heavenly mind.

sections.heading: Confessing my backsliding and wasted opportunities
sections.text: I confess my weakness, my drifting, and my repeated failures. I have not learned as I should from your correction. I have received your mercies, your Word, your worship, and the care of your people without being changed as much as I should have been. I have missed chances to do good, to serve, to speak, to encourage, and to be useful. I grieve that I am not where I once was with you, and I do not want to make peace with that decline.
theological_themes: Backsliding is a real danger in the Christian life.
God’s correction and means of grace are meant to produce growth.
Neglecting opportunities for love and usefulness is part of what repentance must name.

scripture_references.connection: This passage explains God’s discipline as fatherly correction meant to yield holiness, which fits the confession of failing to profit from rebuke.
Paul urges believers not to grow weary in doing good and to use opportunities for service, directly supporting the prayer’s grief over neglected usefulness.

sections.heading: Asking you to bring me back to first love
sections.text: Father, draw me back to yourself. Do not let me settle for distance, dullness, or a divided heart. Wake up the love I had at first—simple, grateful, serious, and glad in you. Let the light you have given me lead to real change. Let the privileges I have received produce deeper repentance, stronger faith, and more faithful obedience.
theological_themes: Restoration comes from God’s gracious initiative.
Love for God can grow cold and needs renewal.
Greater spiritual privilege brings greater responsibility to respond faithfully.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus rebukes the Ephesian church for abandoning its first love and calls it to remember and repent, which closely matches this request for restored affection and obedience.
Jesus teaches that greater entrusted privilege brings greater accountability, supporting the prayer’s desire that growth correspond to what has been received.

sections.heading: Asking for an undivided conscience
sections.text: Make me whole on the inside. Let my will agree with what I know is true. Let my choices match what my conscience, instructed by your Word, approves. Do not let me argue myself into sins I already know are wrong. Keep me from living in a way that condemns me even while I try to defend it. Teach me to put sin to death, not manage it, rename it, or keep it close.
theological_themes: Sanctification includes the alignment of conscience, judgment, will, and action.
Believers must not approve in practice what they know before God to be wrong.
Mortification means actively putting sin to death by God’s grace.

scripture_references.connection: Paul warns against self-condemnation in what one approves and teaches that actions violating conscience are not from faith, making this a strong basis for the prayer’s final request.
Paul calls believers, by the Spirit, to put to death the deeds of the body, grounding the prayer’s desire not merely to feel sorry for sin but to kill it.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses the Puritan category of “means of grace” and assumes that worship, preaching, prayer, and other ordinances can be outwardly attended while inwardly unfruitful. This is broadly Protestant but may be expressed differently across traditions.

The phrase “sins of my holy things” is severe but theologically significant: even religious acts can be polluted by sin. The adaptation preserves this without implying that God rejects sincere worship offered through Christ.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Divine Lawgiver” was rendered as an address to the holy Father whose commands are good, keeping the moral seriousness of God’s law while fitting the prayer’s personal voice.

“It is a day of small things with me” was interpreted as a season of small spiritual vitality, not as despair or unbelief. The adaptation keeps the tension: there is real grace present, but less growth than there should be.
“I have never been straitened in thee” was interpreted to mean that the limitation is not in God’s supply but in the believer’s failure to receive and respond to it.
“May my will accept the decisions of my judgement” was rendered as a request for inner integrity: that conscience, discernment, desire, and action would no longer be divided.
